headline: Every major above its 200-day line, RSI screaming overbought, and whales quietly building exchange balances again
paragraphs: Start with the regime, because it is unusually clean today: six of seven majors, BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP, BNB and DOGE, sit above their 200-day moving average. Only ADA sits below, 76.3% off its 12-month high, the laggard in a market where BTC is 'only' down 37.2% from its own peak. When six of seven crosses agree, you are looking at an uptrend that has broad participation, not one coin dragging the index.

But look at momentum against that trend and you get the first real finding of the day. RSI-14 readings of 81.4 (BTC), 79.6 (ETH), 81.8 (SOL), 81.4 (XRP) and 81.8 (BNB) are deep into overbought territory, the kind of readings that mark a market running hot, not resting. MACD confirms the trend is still up (all seven assets show MACD above signal, ADA included), but overbought-and-rising is a different animal from overbought-and-fresh. BTC's 24.27% seven-day gain and ETH's 32.14% are the kind of moves that get momentum indicators pinned, and pinned indicators tell you the move has been fast, not that it is finished or about to reverse. That is descriptive, not predictive: RSI does not expire trends, it just says they are extended.

Positioning adds texture rather than alarm. Funding across BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP and DOGE perpetuals sits at a uniform 0.01% per 8 hours (11% annualized), a modest, unspectacular cost for longs to carry their bets. That is not the kind of expensive, crowded funding that precedes forced unwinds. The long/short account ratios tell a different story by asset: BTC and ETH sit near parity (1.10, 1.12), but SOL (1.95), XRP (2.09) and especially DOGE (3.40) show crowds heavily tilted long. Liquidation data over the last 9 to 24 hours shows shorts taking the bigger hit on BTC ($10.6M shorts liquidated vs $6.3M longs) and ETH ($8.8M vs $4.3M), consistent with a market still grinding upward and squeezing the skeptics. SOL and XRP flip that pattern, with longs eating more liquidations ($4.5M and $5.1M respectively), a sign those crowded long positions are not free money.

Flows are where the picture gets genuinely two-sided. On 21 Aug, BTC spot ETFs took in $307.5M net, part of a $1,917.8M five-session net with five straight days in the same direction, a real and sustained traditional-finance bid. ETH ETFs echo it: $184.0M on the day, $692.6M over five sessions, also five days running. Stablecoin float, the market's dry powder, is essentially flat over 30 days (+0.01%) at $308.6B, so this buying is not obviously funded by fresh stablecoin issuance. Meanwhile the whale exchange data over the last 48 hours shows $63.5M net moving off exchanges, driven almost entirely by an $88.4M BTC withdrawal from Kraken, while TRUMP token saw $24.9M move onto Binance, a mover-specific flow, not a market-wide one. Zoom out to the weekly view and the trend inverts: the week ending Aug 3 saw $1,141M leave exchanges, but the two weeks after that reversed to $274M and $292M moving onto exchanges, and the week ending Aug 24 shows $1,091M net moving onto exchanges, the largest inflow of the four weeks shown. So the 48-hour snapshot (net outflow, BTC-driven) sits inside a week that, in aggregate, shows the opposite: coins moving back toward exchanges. That is a genuine tension, not a data error, and it is worth sitting with rather than smoothing over.

Sentiment, for once, is not the contrarian signal you'd expect. Fear & Greed reads 73, 'Greed', at the top of its own 30-day range of 25 to 73. Normally a crowd this greedy while whale weekly flows lean toward exchanges would be a classic divergence worth flagging loudly, and it is worth flagging: the crowd feels good, the ETF tape agrees with sustained five-day net buying, but the weekly whale ledger says more coin value is arriving at exchanges than leaving, which is usually where sellers keep their inventory. Worth watching: whether that weekly onto-exchange trend extends into a fifth week, whether ADA can reclaim its 200-day average and join the rest of the pack, and whether funding starts climbing meaningfully above today's flat 11% annualized as a sign leverage is getting more expensive to hold into an already-extended tape.
